objective: At the owner's request ('Yes, let's continue.', approving OPEN-END-GROWTH-20261107-001's recommendation as reframed by the owner: no law chooses anything; ask whether round spaces exist among logical spaces, perhaps only as large-scale trends, and whether roundness differs in kind from polygons). A circle is a bond ball: the distinctions whose least shared knot through a fixed distinction has at most a given size. Serves question 9 (space from a law). Standalone value relative to the nearest known work: periodic graphs have polygonal large-scale balls (Fritz 2013; Kotani-Sunada; Eon), Golab's theorem puts the self-perimeter pi of every normed plane in [3, 4], and first-passage percolation has random limit shapes (Vahidi-Asl-Wierman; Seppalainen); here the distance is bond distance, read from the allowed states of parity laws, and the question is which laws make round circles. A: periodic laws and laws on line arrangements have polygonal circles; a periodic law's pi is rational, regular only for the hexagon (3) and the parallelogram (4); n equiangular line families give regular 2n-gons with Archimedes' values of pi; exact table for the Archimedean and Laves laws. B: splitting each knot of the square law into two atoms by independent coins bends the circle (exact elliptic corners, circular for fair coins); an isotropic random law of atoms has an exactly round circle. C: exploratory measurements of circles of random laws (Voronoi law, uniform random planar law, finite-size split law).
status: Complete 2026-11-07: circles from logic. Round spaces exist among logical spaces, but no periodic law and no coin-split lattice law makes one. Periodic laws have polygonal circles whose pi (Golab's half self-perimeter) is rational; by Niven's theorem only the hexagon (pi = 3) and parallelogram (pi = 4) are regular (proved; 19 Archimedean and Laves laws computed exactly, pi in {3, 10/3, 16/5, 7/2, 11/3, 4}). Laws on n line directions give regular 2n-gons with Archimedes' pi, reaching the circle only as n grows; Penrose gives 5/phi (proved). Splitting each knot of the square law into two three-place knots by coins gives a square with elliptic corners, exact quarter circles for fair coins, pi = 3.44120 (proved, citing Seppalainen 1997); a Poisson-Voronoi law of three-place knots is exactly round (proved, isotropy); a uniform random planar law is not a plane (measured n^0.28). Next: Continue (2/3), round without coins: the pinwheel law.
stop_rule: Stop when the circles of five families are classified (periodic laws, aperiodic line-arrangement laws, lattice laws with random splits, isotropic random laws, uniform random planar laws) as polygon with exact pi, curved with exact shape, round, or not a plane; do not tune a law toward roundness after seeing results.
title: Circles from logic: polygons, coins and roundness
